stage1_evidence_shown.label: OBJECTIVE
stage1_evidence_shown.context: To investigate the ability of a bedside swallowing assessment to reliably exclude aspiration following acute stroke.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: SUBJECTS
stage1_evidence_shown.context: Consecutive patients admitted within 24 h of stroke onset to two hospitals.

stage1_evidence_shown.label: METHODS
stage1_evidence_shown.context: A prospective study. Where possible, all patients had their ability to swallow assessed on the day of admission by both a doctor and a speech and language therapist using a standardized proforma. A videofluoroscopy examination was conducted within 3 days of admission.

stage2_added_evidence.label: RESULTS
stage2_added_evidence.context: 94 patients underwent videofluoroscopy; 20 (21%) were seen to be aspirating, although this was not detected at the bedside in 10. In 18 (22%) of the patients the speech and language therapist considered the swallow to be unsafe. In the medical assessment, 39 patients (41%) had an unsafe swallow. Bedside assessment by a speech and language therapist gave a sensitivity of 47%, a specificity of 86%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 50% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 85% for the presence of aspiration. Multiple logistic regression was used to identify the optimum elements of the bedside assessments for predicting the presence of aspiration. A weak voluntary cough and any alteration in conscious level gave a sensitivity of 75%, specificity of 72%, PPV of 41% and NPV of 91% for aspiration.
